title: Five Constitutional Writs in PIL — Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Certiorari, Prohibition and Quo Warranto

content.overview: PIL uses the same five constitutional writs available under Articles 32 and 226 — habeas corpus, mandamus, certiorari, prohibition, and quo warranto — with liberalised standing. Choosing the correct writ matches the wrong: detention, public duty, jurisdictional error, or usurped office.
content.glance: Ask: (1) Detention of liberty? (2) Public duty not performed? (3) Order without jurisdiction or illegality? (4) Proceedings to be stopped? (5) Office held without authority?
content.study:
Core rule: PIL is standing and process, not a sixth writ. Relief is still framed through the recognised writs or equivalent directions under Articles 32 and 226.

Habeas corpus: unlawful detention; often used for missing persons or illegal custody claims in public-interest settings.

Mandamus: compel performance of a public duty; the workhorse of structural PIL, including continuing mandamus forms.

Certiorari: quash orders of bodies acting without or in excess of jurisdiction or with patent illegality.

Prohibition: stop inferior bodies from exceeding jurisdiction.

Quo warranto: challenge usurpation of a public office.

Current-law framing: Match facts to the writ; standing liberalisation does not change writ ingredients. Verification of holdings remains separate.

sections.heading: Writs as the relief vocabulary of PIL
sections.body: Public-interest standing opens the door; the five writs (or directions of like nature) supply the remedy. Answers should name the writ that fits the pleaded wrong.

sections.heading: Habeas corpus in public-interest settings
sections.body: Used where liberty is restrained without lawful authority. Representative petitioners may seek production of persons who cannot approach the court.

sections.heading: Mandamus and continuing directions
sections.body: Mandamus compels public duties. Where default is ongoing, courts may structure successive monitoring directions (continuing mandamus) within the same writ power.

sections.heading: Certiorari and prohibition
sections.body: Certiorari quashes completed or operative orders tainted by jurisdictional error or illegality. Prohibition restrains further excess of jurisdiction. Both require a body amenable to writ and a jurisdictional or legal defect.

sections.heading: Quo warranto
sections.body: Challenges occupation of a public office without legal authority. Public interest in lawful tenure of office can support standing where the office is public.

High Court power to issue writs

examples.title: Duty default
examples.body: Authorities fail to operate a statutory welfare scheme for a class of beneficiaries. Mandamus (possibly continuing) is the fit writ language.

examples.title: Illegal detention claim
examples.body: A representative petition seeks production of persons allegedly held without authority. Habeas corpus is the fit writ.

hypotheticals.question: Does PIL create a new writ beyond the five?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. PIL liberalises standing and process; relief is still through the constitutional writs or equivalent directions.

distinctions.title: Writ choice vs standing
distinctions.left: Writ choice: which remedy fits the wrong.
distinctions.right: Standing: who may ask for that remedy in public interest.

misconceptions.trap: Any PIL can demand any writ without matching facts.
misconceptions.correction: Each writ has ingredients; mismatch is a ground for refusal.

cases.name: Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India
cases.ratioDecidendi: Courts may use flexible procedure and continuing directions for effective rights enforcement.
cases.holding: Petition treated as vehicle for Article 21 enforcement.

cases.name: S.P. Gupta v. Union of India
cases.issue: When may a person approach for public injury?
cases.ratioDecidendi: Standing may be relaxed for bona fide public redress.
cases.relevance: Standing context for writ petitions; verification open.

cases.name: State of Uttaranchal v. Balwant Singh Chaufal
cases.ratioDecidendi: Verify credentials, motive, public injury, absence of personal gain.
cases.relevance: Maintainability before writ relief; verification open.
